statement: crates/enforcer-harness/src/ci_parity.rs parses GitHub Actions workflow YAML with a minimal, hand-rolled line scanner (recognizes `- name:`, `uses: owner/action@ref`, and a `# ci-parity: <tool>=<version>` comment convention for pins hidden inside free-form `run:` shell commands) instead of adding a YAML crate dependency. The workspace carried zero YAML crates before this workpack (grep across crates/ and Cargo.lock confirmed).
why: The only surface this module needs from a workflow file is step names plus a narrow pinned-version hint; a full YAML parser is heavier and less auditable than a purpose-built scanner for that one shape, and avoids adding a new dependency to enforcer-harness purely for this.
howToApply: A future workpack (e.g. d28 target-ci-parity, which audits arbitrary TARGET repos' CI workflows and therefore cannot assume this same narrow shape) may need a real YAML parser -- if so, evaluate serde_yml/saphyr at that point rather than assuming d11's hand-rolled scanner generalizes to arbitrary third-party workflow files.

statement: This workspace's clippy::expect_used/unwrap_used=deny gate has zero #[allow] tolerance in some task briefs even though the codebase's OWN established precedent (enforcer-mechanization::parity::diagnostic_relpath) uses a scoped #[allow(clippy::expect_used)] for a provably-infallible literal parse of a branded type (RuleId/RelPath have no infallible public constructor by design -- validate-on-construction doctrine). When a task brief says 'zero #[allow]' but the codebase precedent uses one, prefer the stricter reading: replace the literal-parse-then-expect pattern with a fallible helper (e.g. `fn push_x(out: &mut Vec<T>, ...)` that parses into a `Result` and only pushes/acts on `Ok`, silently and safely no-oping on the theoretically-unreachable `Err` arm) plus a dedicated unit test asserting the literal parses today, rather than reaching for #[allow] or (worse) a recursive retry-fallback function which trades a panic for a stack-overflow risk and is strictly worse.
why: A caller-specified stricter bar than the codebase's own established pattern should win for the files that caller owns -- but the fix must still be genuinely safe, not a superficial dodge (a recursive fallback-literal parse 'to avoid expect' is a regression, not a fix).
howToApply: For any RuleId/RelPath (or other TryFrom<String>-only branded type) construction from a fixed literal inside a #[allow]-free file: push the fallible parse into a small helper taking a mutable output collection (or returning Option/Result) and handling the Err arm by doing nothing (documented as unreachable-in-practice, backed by a unit test on the literal), never by unwrap/expect/panic or by retrying the same fallible parse recursively.

evidence.ref: cargo clippy -p enforcer-harness --all-targets -- -D warnings: 2 expect_used errors surfaced on rule_id()/manifest_relpath() helpers before refactor to push_step_finding()
